content.title: The last step of the recipe
content.text: Multiply, add, add the bias: a straight line in every input, as the previous pill showed. Then the squash, the last step of a neuron and the one that undoes the collapse. The squash is itself a function: one number in, z, one number out. This neuron’s z is 0.235; after the squash it sends on 0.231. Almost the same here. The squash only shows its hand further out.

content.title: The S-curve: tanh
content.text: The squash this network uses is called tanh, and its picture is an S. Near zero it is almost the line y = z: small totals pass through nearly untouched. Further out it flattens: whatever comes in, what goes out stays between −1 and 1. A total of 2 becomes 0.964, 4 becomes 0.999, and 40 becomes 1.000 as well. This neuron sits near the middle. Neuron 23 of the same row, with z = 1.38, is already at 0.88, close to the ceiling.

content.title: The hinge: ReLU
content.text: The other squash in common use is called ReLU, and its picture is a hinge. A negative total: out comes 0. A positive total: out comes the number itself, untouched. Not a range from 0 to 1: zero, or the number. A hard floor on the left, no ceiling on the right. It is also the cheapest thing a computer can do to a number, a single comparison.

content.title: A line through the squash
content.text: Back to the line of the previous pill: turn the weight on this pixel’s wire from −6 to 6 and z runs on a straight line, from −3.82 to 3.68. Now pass that line through the squash. Through tanh it becomes an S: flat near −1, a climb through the middle, flat near 1. Through the hinge it becomes 0 on the whole left half and the line itself on the right. Either way the line is bent, and a bent line is something new.

content.title: What the bend buys
content.text: Pick one weight of the first row, the wire from this bright pixel to neuron 4, and turn it from −6 to 6 while watching the raw score for 7 at the far end of the network. With the squash in every neuron the score climbs from 1.03 to 1.40 and falls back to 1.20: up, then down. No straight line can do that, and no stack of straight lines can either. Take every squash out and the same turn gives a line, 1.67 to 2.55, forever up. The bend is what lets the rows add up to more than one line.

content.title: Which squash, and why
content.text: This small network uses tanh, and for a long time most networks did. Most large networks today use the hinge or a close cousin of it, for two reasons. The hinge is cheap, one comparison where tanh needs an exponential, and a large network does this billions of times. And the S flattens at both ends: far out, its slope is nearly zero, so big totals all look alike, and that matters for learning, which runs on slopes. The hinge keeps slope 1 on its whole right side.

content.title: The recipe, complete
content.text: Multiply, add, add the bias, squash: that is the entire neuron, and now every step has a shape. The weights are slopes, the bias is a lift, the squash is a bend. The 58 neurons of this network all do exactly this; the ten in the last row only add a squash of their own that turns ten raw scores into percentages adding up to 100. What is left is choosing the numbers: how to measure how wrong they are, and which way to turn each one.
